meta.tagline: Duolingo won't teach you this — Germany edition (plus Bayern mode).

categories.title: Ordering a beer/food like a local (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You're at a German bar and they ask what you'd like to drink.

question.en: What would you like to drink? (formal Sie)

answers.en: A pale lager, please — common in the south.

likelyReply.es: Vom Fass oder aus der Flasche?

exchanges.notes: "Ein Helles" is the southern default. Servers open with the formal Sie.

situation.en: You've ordered a beer and they ask how you want it.

question.es: Vom Fass oder aus der Flasche?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: In a Munich beer garden, they ask what size beer you want.

exchanges.notes: Size is its own question, asked after you've said what you want and whether it's draft. It's a Bavarian one: a Maß is the liter stein, a Halbe the half-liter. Order a Maß in Hamburg and you'll get a look. Die Maß is feminine, so it's eine Maß, not einen.

situation.en: They ask whether you want something to eat as well.

question.es: Möchten Sie auch was zu essen?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You're paying as a group and they ask how.

exchanges.notes: Splitting the bill is completely normal and expected.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You want to know which beers they have on draft before you choose.

question.en: What have you got on tap?

answers.en: Pils, pale lager and a wheat beer.

exchanges.notes: Asking this rather than pointing at a tap handle is most of the difference.

situation.en: Your glass is empty and the server catches your eye.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: It's late and the bartender offers you one last small drink.

answers.es: Nein, ich muss morgen früh raus.
answers.en: No, I've got an early start.

exchanges.notes: Ein Absacker is the last drink of the night — literally the one that makes you sink.

categories.title: Starting a convo/basic survival (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: Someone greets you.
Someone asks how you're doing.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You need help and want to check whether they speak English.

exchanges.notes: "Sprechen Sie Englisch?" is the formal version — use it with staff, officials and anyone much older. Same question, different register.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You didn't catch what someone just said.

exchanges.notes: "Ich check's nicht" is casual — fine with peers, not in a formal setting.

situation.en: You don't know a word and want to ask what it is.

question.en: How do you say [WORD] in German?

situation.en: You're looking for a place and stop someone to ask.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: A German friend greets you with a single syllable and then waits.

answers.en: Hey! — mirroring it back is the correct answer.

exchanges.notes: "Na?" is a complete greeting on its own. Answering "Na!" is not a dodge — it is the reply.

situation.en: You've been chatting a while and realize you never said your name.

note.es: Slang level: medium → heavy. Items marked young are more common with younger people, online, and in friend groups.
note.en: If you want local but safe, use the ones without a young badge. Items marked very casual are not for work.

phrases.en: Intense / crazy / wow.
Awesome. Can sound crude in other contexts, but common as "cool".
Super.
For sure.
Solid / good.
It's going / all good.
Awesome — literally "hammer".
Insane / unbelievable — good or bad, tone decides.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend tells you they cycled across the country in four days.

question.en: Four days, right across the country.

scenes.notes: Krass covers impressive, shocking and appalling. The tone picks which, and it is the single most used slang word in German.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone plays you the track they've been talking about all week.

scenes.notes: Geil literally means horny and nobody hears that any more in this use. Still worth knowing before you say it to a colleague.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone you haven't seen in a while asks how things are going.

question.es: Und sonst so? Alles gut bei dir?
question.en: And otherwise? All fine with you?

scenes.notes: Läuft is the short version, and among younger people it is often the whole answer: läuft, said with a shrug.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend tells you they got tickets for the sold-out show.

likelyReply.es: Ich weiß, ich freu mich so.

scenes.notes: Literally a hammer. Said on its own, and der Hammer as a noun does the same job: das war der Hammer.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone tells you the queue for the club went round two corners.

question.es: Die Schlange ging um zwei Ecken.
question.en: The queue went round two corners.

likelyReply.en: We went home in the end.

scenes.notes: Wahnsinn is madness, and it works for both good and bad news. The tone is the whole difference.

phrases.en: (Not) in the mood / up for it.
I'm in.
I can't be bothered with that.
Do you fancy it?
Definitely — clipped from "auf jeden Fall".
I'd rather not.
Doesn't work for me right now.
I'm out — count me out of this one.

situation.en: A plan is coming together and everyone is saying whether they're coming.

question.es: Wir fahren Samstag an den See.
question.en: We're driving to the lake on Saturday.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody suggests a museum on the one afternoon you wanted to do nothing.

question.en: Shall we go to the museum?

answers.en: I can't be bothered with that.

scenes.notes: Bock is the word for wanting to do something at all. Keinen Bock is blunt but not rude among friends.

situation.en: You've got a spare ticket and want to ask somebody along without making it a thing.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone offers you a schnapps at eleven in the morning.

scenes.notes: The softest refusal in the section: it declines the thing without declining the person.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: The group is planning a third night out in a row and counting heads.

scenes.notes: Ich bin raus is out of this particular plan, not out of the friendship. Borrowed from card games.

phrases.en: Dude! / bro! — tone matters.
Bro / dude. Very casual.
Brother — used like mate, mostly among young men.
Guys! — the safe one for a whole group.
Man! — frustration or emphasis, never a word for a person.
Mate — jokey and slightly ironic between friends.
Love / hon — partners and close family only.
Lads / girls — calling over a mixed group.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend tells you they left their phone in the taxi that just drove off.

scenes.notes: Alter is literally 'old one' and means nothing of the kind. Tone is everything: warm it is mate, flat it is a warning.

scenes.speaker: you

situation.en: You want the whole table's attention to say where you're going next.

scenes.notes: Leute is the safe one for a mixed group of any age. Jungs and Mädels split it by gender; Leute never has to.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: The train you needed has been cancelled for the second time today.

scenes.notes: Mann here is frustration, never a word for a person. Mensch does the same job a shade more gently.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend turns up with exactly the tool you needed and no explanation.

scenes.notes: Not your actual colleague. Between friends it is jokey and slightly ironic, like calling somebody 'chief'.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Your partner has brought you coffee without being asked.

scenes.notes: Schatz is treasure, and it is for partners and close family only. Said to a stranger it is either flirting or an insult.

phrases.en: No idea. Shortened to "kp" in texts.
I swear.
Are you clueless? Can come across as rude.
Exactly — and, just as often, pure filler while they think.
Ohh, I see — the realization noise.
Seriously?
Nonsense! / rubbish!
Yes and no — ja plus nein, and a real dictionary word.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Nobody at the table believes the story you've just told.

scenes.notes: Very young and very common. Among people over thirty it will get you a look.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone works out for themselves the thing you were trying to explain.

question.es: Also erst die U-Bahn, dann der Bus?
question.en: So the U-Bahn first, then the bus?

scenes.notes: Also filler. A German will say genau three times while deciding what to say next, and it means nothing at all those times.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've been confused for five minutes and somebody finally explains why.

question.en: The shop is closed on Sundays.

likelyReply.es: Ja, hier ist sonntags alles zu.
likelyReply.en: Yes — everything's shut here on Sundays.

scenes.notes: The realization noise, and one of the first things you'll catch yourself saying without deciding to.

situation.en: A friend says they're moving to another country in three weeks.

question.es: Ich zieh in drei Wochen weg.
question.en: I'm moving away in three weeks.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone claims the beer here is cheaper than the water.

question.es: Bier ist billiger als Wasser hier.
question.en: Beer is cheaper than water here.

scenes.notes: Quatsch is rubbish, said about the claim rather than the person, which is what keeps it friendly.

categories.title: Bayern slang / Bavarian flavor
categories.description: Identity language for Bavaria and parts of Austria

note.es: Standard German works everywhere. Bavarian is regional identity language — use it in Bayern and Austria.
note.en: Don't drop it in Hamburg and expect the same vibe. Outside the south you'll sound very regional.

phrases.en: Hi / bye (informal).
Good day — the standard southern greeting, safe with anyone.
Bye — singular / plural.
Hello, to one person — warmer and more local than Servus.
Hello, to a group.
Pleased to meet you — literally "I have the honour".
Goodbye — the southern version of auf Wiedersehen.
Hello everyone — greeting a whole table at once.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You walk into a bakery in Munich and the woman behind the counter looks up.

question.en: Good day — what can I get you?

scenes.notes: Standard German, not dialect, and safe with absolutely anyone in the south. Hallo marks you as a northerner within one word.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend's grandfather greets you at the door of a village house.

scenes.notes: Warmer and more local than Servus, and for one person only. Say it to a table and you have said the wrong thing.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You arrive at a table of six in a beer garden and they all look up at once.

scenes.notes: The plural of Griaß di. Bavarian keeps the singular and the plural apart where English gave up, and getting it right is noticed.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're introduced to somebody's father, who puts out his hand.

scenes.notes: Literally 'I have the honour', squashed into one word. Old-fashioned, slightly formal, and it will make a Bavarian smile.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're leaving a shop in a small Bavarian town with your bag.

question.en: Goodbye and have a lovely day!

scenes.notes: The southern auf Wiedersehen, and what you will actually hear in a shop. Tschüss is northern and sounds it.

phrases.en: Emphasis particle — roughly "you know" / "mind you" / "really".
Sighing interjection: "oh man…".
Nonsense! — literally a shredded pancake.
Don't rush! — a whole philosophy in two words.
We'll see — the Bavarian shrug.
A little bit.
Daft, silly — mild enough to say to a friend.
A professional grump — said with real affection.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody insists the Oktoberfest beer is watered down.

question.es: Des Bier is verdünnt, sag i dir.
question.en: That beer's watered down, I'm telling you.

scenes.notes: A Schmarrn is a shredded pancake. As an exclamation it is rubbish, nonsense, and it is used far more often than the pudding is eaten.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody is trying to hurry you through a meal you are enjoying.

question.en: Come on, we've got to go!

scenes.notes: Two words holding an entire attitude to time. Said to anybody in a hurry, with complete sincerity.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're asked to commit to a plan for a weekend three months away.

question.en: Are you coming along in August?

scenes.notes: Literally 'let's have a look'. It is the Bavarian shrug, and it is neither a yes nor a no on purpose.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody is pouring and asks how much you want.

scenes.notes: A bisserl is ein bisschen, southern. The -erl ending is all over Bavarian and makes everything smaller and fonder.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend has walked into the same glass door twice in one evening.

scenes.notes: Deppert is daft, and mild enough to say to a friend's face. A Depp is the person; deppert is how they are being.

phrases.en: It's fine / all good.
I like you — dialect-y.
We are who we are — Bavaria's unofficial motto.
The bread-and-cold-cuts meal — a fixed part of the day, not a snack.
A bread roll — a Brötchen everywhere north of here.
A half-liter of beer — the everyday order, not the tourist liter.
Beer with lemonade — orderable anywhere in Bayern without comment.
Squirrel's tail — the pronunciation test a local will eventually set you.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've apologized twice for being forty cents short and they've stopped listening.

scenes.notes: The most Bavarian two words there are: it is fine, leave it, do not make it a thing. Also what you say instead of keeping the change.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's late at the Wiesn and somebody has been waiting for you to say something.

scenes.notes: Dialect for ich mag dich, and it carries more weight down here than the standard version does. Not a thing to say lightly.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're at a Munich bakery counter and the word you learned in Berlin is the wrong one.

scenes.notes: A Semmel in Bayern, a Schrippe in Berlin, a Brötchen in most of the rest. Same roll, three words, and locals notice which you use.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're in a beer garden and want the size the locals are drinking.

scenes.notes: A Hoibe is the half-liter, and it is what most people at the table are actually drinking. The liter Maß is for the Wiesn and for tourists.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's a hot afternoon and you want something you can drink two of.

scenes.notes: Beer with lemonade, named after the cyclists it was invented for. Orderable anywhere in Bayern without a single raised eyebrow.

note.es: Profanity is common, but don't use it with strangers unless you really know the vibe.

phrases.en: Shit.
Damn.
A milder "crap".
Man! / oh come on! — completely safe in any company.
Darn! — the polite one.
Bloody hell — stronger than Verdammt, and still aimed at nobody.
Good heavens!
Well I never! — admiration or annoyance, tone decides which.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: The connection you were running for pulls out of the platform as you arrive.

likelyReply.es: Der nächste geht in zwanzig Minuten.
likelyReply.en: The next one's in twenty minutes.

scenes.notes: The workhorse. Common enough to be barely rude, and still not for a job interview.

situation.en: You get to the front of the queue and your card is in the other jacket.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It starts raining ten minutes into a walk and nobody brought a jacket.

scenes.notes: Mist is manure and lands about where 'crap' does. The one to reach for in front of somebody's parents.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone has spent ten minutes trying to explain the ticket machine to you.

question.es: Und dann noch einmal von vorne.
question.en: And now once more from the top.

answers.en: Oh man — now I've got it.

scenes.notes: Completely safe in any company, including at work and in front of children. Frustration or affection, depending on the tone.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend tells you they swam across the lake and back before breakfast.

scenes.notes: Literally a thunderstorm. Admiration here; said flatly at somebody it is a telling-off, and both are old-fashioned in a likeable way.

phrases.en: Shut it.
Piss off.
Leave me alone — firm, and not a swear word.
Stop bugging me.
That's enough now.
Oh sh*t! — a reaction to a situation, not aimed at a person.
Total idiot — keep it for telling the story, not for the person.
Get lost — everyday among friends, never with a stranger.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody has been talking over you for ten minutes and starts up again.

question.es: Nein, jetzt hörst du mir mal zu.
question.en: No — now you listen to me.

scenes.notes: Genuinely rude. Among close friends it can be a joke; with anybody else it is the start of a row.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone has followed you down the street after being told twice to stop.

question.en: Come on, don't be like that.

scenes.notes: The strong one, and the one to keep for when you mean it. Lass mich in Ruhe does the same job without the swear.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody at the bar will not take a polite no for an answer.

scenes.notes: Not a swear word, and firmer for it. Clear enough that anybody listening knows exactly what was said.

situation.en: A friend has made the same joke at your expense four times tonight.

question.es: Und dann noch mal mit dem Akzent!

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Your friend shows you the state of the kitchen after the party.

scenes.notes: Aimed at a situation, never at a person, which is what makes it safe where the others are not.

categories.title: Calling someone attractive (Germany)
categories.description: Flirt lines that don't land badly

note.es: Only flirt if it feels mutual. Keep it light and accept a no immediately.
note.en: Back off without arguing or guilt-tripping.

phrases.en: You look good.
You're really cute.
I like your style.
You have a nice smile.
You have beautiful eyes.
You've got a lovely laugh.

phrases.es: Mit dir kann man gut reden.
phrases.en: You're easy to talk to.
I really like you — warm, and not a come-on.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone you like arrives at the bar and takes their coat off.

scenes.notes: The plain one, and it works. Gut aussehen is about how somebody looks tonight rather than a verdict on them.

situation.en: They get flustered ordering and apologize for it.

question.en: Sorry — I'm all over the place.

situation.en: Someone mentions they put the whole outfit together second-hand.

question.en: All from the flea market, honestly.

situation.en: They laugh at something you said and you want to say what you noticed.
You've been talking across a table with a candle on it for an hour.

question.en: Why are you looking at me like that?

phrases.en: I find you attractive.

phrases.es: Hast du Lust auf ein Bier?
phrases.en: Want to grab a beer?
I like you.
Shall we go somewhere else?
Are you staying a bit longer?
I'd love to see you again.
Can I have your number?

phrases.es: Das war ein schöner Abend mit dir.
phrases.en: That was a lovely evening with you.

situation.en: They ask, half joking, why you keep looking over.

question.es: Warum guckst du eigentlich immer her?
question.en: Why do you keep looking over here?

situation.en: The group is splitting up and you'd like to see this one person again.

question.es: Ich glaub, ich fahr dann heim.
question.en: I think I'll head home, then.

answers.es: Hast du Lust auf ein Bier?

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: They ask what this actually is, directly, because it is late and nobody is pretending.

scenes.notes: Mögen is to like and here it means it. Lieben is a long way further on and not a first-night word in German either.

situation.en: The music has got loud enough that you're both shouting.
Their friends are at the door and you have about five seconds.

question.en: I have to go with them.

phrases.en: No pressure if not.
All good, I respect that.
Honestly, no problem.
I'll leave you to it.
It was good to meet you.
All good — enjoy your night.
Sorry, I misread that.
I didn't mean to be pushy.

situation.en: You've suggested carrying on somewhere else and they've gone quiet.
They tell you they're seeing somebody already.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: They've given one-word answers twice and are looking at their phone.

question.es: Sorry, ich bin heut nicht so da.
question.en: Sorry — I'm not really here tonight.

scenes.notes: Leaving cleanly is the skill. Said once, without a sigh, and then actually done.

situation.en: You read the evening as going one way and it was going another.

question.en: I honestly just wanted to talk.

situation.en: You realize you've been standing closer than they are comfortable with.

question.en: A bit of space would be good.

answers.en: I didn't mean to be pushy.

phrases.en: Can I tell you something?

phrases.es: Ist es okay, wenn ich dich auf einen Drink einlade?
phrases.en: Is it okay if I ask you for a drink?
Is this okay with you?
Do you want me to go?

phrases.es: Sag einfach, wenn's zu viel ist.
phrases.en: Just say if it's too much.
May I sit down?
Would you rather be on your own?
Are you comfortable with this?

situation.en: Their glass is empty and you're already halfway to standing up.

answers.es: Ist es okay, wenn ich dich auf einen Drink einlade?
answers.en: Is it okay if I buy you a drink?

situation.en: You've put an arm along the back of the bench they're sitting on.
Their friends have arrived and the mood at the table has changed.

answers.en: Do you want me to go?

situation.en: There's one free chair at the table and you've been talking across the room.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: They've been looking out of the window rather than at the party for a while.

answers.en: Would you rather be on your own?

scenes.notes: Offering the exit is the point. Asked once and accepted without an argument is the whole difference.

categories.title: Getting around (taxi + metro) (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've landed and you're looking for where the taxis are.

question.en: Where do I find a taxi?

answers.en: Outside, in front of the exit.

exchanges.notes: Works for the bus and the train too — swap Taxi for Bus or Zug.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: Before getting in, you want to know what a taxi into town costs.

question.en: What does it cost to the center?

exchanges.notes: Ask before the bags go in the boot, not after.

situation.en: You've landed and want the train into the city rather than a taxi.

question.es: Wo ist der Zug in die Stadt?
question.en: Where's the train into the city?

situation.en: An officer at the border asks for your documents.

answers.en: One moment, I'll get it out.

situation.en: You need to collect your suitcase and can't see which way to go.
You want a transport ticket and can't find anywhere to buy one.

question.es: Wo kann ich ein Ticket kaufen?
question.en: Where can I buy a ticket?

situation.en: Customs stops you on the way out of the airport.
You have your bag and just need to get out of the terminal.
You get into a taxi and the driver asks where to.
You've arrived and want the driver to pull over.
You're at the taxi with a heavy suitcase and need the boot opened.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You've arrived and the driver asks how you're settling up.

question.es: Zahlen Sie bar oder mit Karte?
question.en: Are you paying cash or card?

exchanges.notes: Plenty of German taxis are still cash-first. Ask before you get in if you have no notes.

situation.en: You've spotted your street and want to get out before the corner.
You're running late and want to know how long the ride will take.

question.en: Roughly how long will it take?

situation.en: You need the fare receipted so you can expense the trip.
The driver reads the address back to you before setting off.
You're on the street looking for the U-Bahn.
You know your destination but not which line to take.

question.en: I need to go to [PLACE]. Which line?

situation.en: You're on the platform and want to know if the line goes straight there.
You're on board and want to know how far your stop is.
It's well past midnight and you don't know if the line is still running.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: An inspector in plain clothes asks to see your ticket mid-journey.

exchanges.notes: German metros have no barriers — inspectors board at random and a missing ticket is a 60-euro fine.

situation.en: Two platforms serve the same line and you don't know which one you want.
You're on a platform and want someone to confirm you're on the right side.

question.es: Ist das hier die richtige Seite?
question.en: Am I on the right side?

categories.title: At a restaurant (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You arrive at a restaurant with one other person.

question.es: Haben Sie einen Tisch für zwei?

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've finished eating and want to pay.

exchanges.notes: Cash is still common — plenty of places are card-shy.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You want tap water rather than bottled.

exchanges.notes: Tap water isn't automatic in Germany — you have to ask for it by name.

situation.en: You've been at the table a few minutes and the server comes over.

likelyReply.en: I'll come back in a moment.

situation.en: The menu means nothing to you and you'd rather be told what's good.

answers.en: The schnitzel is the most popular.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've decided and want to order your main course.

answers.en: Of course. Anything to drink with that?

exchanges.notes: "Ich hätte gern" is the polite default for ordering anything, food or drink.

situation.en: A plate arrives that isn't what you asked for.

question.es: Entschuldigung, das habe ich nicht bestellt.
question.en: Excuse me, I didn't order this.

answers.es: Oh, Entschuldigung — ich tausche es um.

situation.en: The server clears your plate and asks how the food was.

categories.title: Checking in (hotel/hostel/Airbnb) (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You arrive at the hotel desk and need to claim your booking.

question.es: Ich habe eine Reservierung auf den Namen [NAME].

answers.en: One moment, I'll look it up.

likelyReply.es: Kann ich bitte Ihren Pass sehen?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You walk in without booking ahead and they ask at the desk.

answers.es: Nein, haben Sie noch ein Zimmer frei?
answers.en: No, do you have a room free?

exchanges.notes: The situation is that you did not book, so the line to reach for is the one that says so. "Ja, für zwei Nächte" is here too because the same question gets asked of people who did book.

situation.en: You want to know whether breakfast costs extra.

answers.es: Nein, das kostet zehn Euro extra.

situation.en: You're planning your last morning and need the checkout time.

question.en: When do I have to check out?

situation.en: Your train is this evening but the room is gone at eleven.

question.en: Can I leave my luggage here?

answers.es: Klar, wir stellen es in den Gepäckraum.
answers.en: Sure, we'll put it in the luggage room.

situation.en: You're in the room and want to get online.
They hand you the key and tell you where to go.

answers.en: Two streets down there's an Italian place.

situation.en: The room is freezing and the radiator is doing nothing.

answers.en: I'll send someone up right away.

answers.es: Das tut mir leid — ich melde es sofort.
answers.en: I'm sorry — I'll report it right away.

question.es: Können Sie mich um sieben wecken?

answers.es: Kein Thema, ich komme mit hoch.
answers.en: Not a problem, I'll come up with you.

question.en: Can we stay one more night?

answers.en: I'll see whether the room is free.

situation.en: You're handing the key back and they ask about your stay.

question.en: Do you have this one size bigger?

You're at the till with an armful and no bag.

exchanges.speaker: you

exchanges.notes: Sunday closing is near-total in Germany. Plan Saturday, or find a Späti or a station shop.

situation.en: You hand over a fifty for a four-euro shop.

exchanges.speaker: you

answers.en: Back left, next to the entrance.

You're deciding between two bottles and want to know which one you get money back on.

The cashier asks about a loyalty card before ringing you up.

question.en: Do I have to weigh the fruit myself?

categories.title: Berlin slang / Berliner Schnauze
categories.description: The capital's own dialect — blunt, fast and warm underneath.

note.es: Die Berliner Schnauze klingt grob und ist es nicht.
note.en: Berliners sound brusque and mean nothing by it. The bluntness is the friendliness — take it at face value and answer in kind.

subsections.title: Berlinerisch — the words that give it away

phrases.en: I — Berlin's own version of ich.
What — wat and det replace was and das.
That — Berlin's das.
Brilliant — old Berlin, still said with a wink.
Great — same vintage as knorke, same wink.
Not happening — "gibt es nicht" in a Berlin mouth.
Eh? / right? — the tag stuck on the end of everything.
Look at that! — "guck mal" up here.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone behind the Späti counter says something you don't catch.

likelyReply.es: Ick sach, dit kostet zwei Euro.

scenes.notes: Berlin turns was into wat and das into det, and it does it in nearly every sentence. Reading it is harder than hearing it.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're at an Imbiss counter pointing at something you don't know the name of.

scenes.notes: Det is Berlin's das. Pointing and saying det da will get you fed anywhere in the city.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend shows you the roof terrace that comes with their flat.

question.es: Und det jehört alles zur Wohnung.
question.en: And all this comes with the flat.

scenes.notes: Old Berlin, and still said — usually with a wink, because everybody knows how old it is.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone asks whether there's a direct train out to the lake on a Sunday.

scenes.notes: Gibt es nicht, in a Berlin mouth. The g goes to a j and the whole thing collapses into one word.

scenes.speaker: you

situation.en: You spot something on the far side of the canal worth pointing out.

scenes.notes: Guck mal, up here. Kieken is the Berlin verb for looking, and you will hear it before you ever need to say it.

subsections.title: Späti, Kiez and what things are called here

phrases.en: The late-night corner shop — a Berlin institution and your 2am friend.
Your neighborhood — Berliners identify with theirs more than with the city.
A bread roll — a Brötchen elsewhere, a Semmel in Bayern.
A jam doughnut. A pancake here is an Eierkuchen — order carefully.
A meat patty — a Frikadelle in most of the country.
A sandwich — a buttered slice with something on top.
A beer for the walk — legal in public and completely unremarkable.
The corner pub — cheap, old, open late, and nothing like a bar.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's two in the morning and the party has run out of everything.

scenes.notes: The late-night corner shop, open when nothing else is, and the reason a Berlin evening never quite has to end.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're at a Berlin bakery and the word you learned in Munich is the wrong one.

scenes.notes: A Schrippe in Berlin, a Semmel in Bayern, a Brötchen almost everywhere else. Same roll, and the word places you instantly.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You want a jam doughnut and the word for it here is not the word you expect.

scenes.notes: A Pfannkuchen is a doughnut in Berlin and a pancake almost everywhere else. Ask for one in Munich and you get a pancake.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody asks what you want to take to the park.

scenes.notes: A Stulle is a buttered slice with something on it, and the word is northern. Down south it is a belegtes Brot.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're walking to the next bar and someone offers to stop at the Späti on the way.

answers.es: Ja, ich hol mir ein Wegbier.
answers.en: Yes — I'll get a beer for the walk.

scenes.notes: Drinking in public is legal here and entirely unremarkable. The bottle opener on the Späti counter is there for exactly this.

categories.title: Nightlife — the door, the club, the people (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You reach the front of the queue and the bouncer counts your group.
The bouncer looks at you and wants to know your age.
You're at the front and want to know what you'll be paying.

question.en: How much is it to get in?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: The bouncer looks past you and turns you away without a reason.

answers.en: Fair enough, have a good night.

exchanges.notes: Berlin doors give no reason and you do not ask for one. Taking it well is the entire etiquette — arguing guarantees it again.

situation.en: It's early and you want to know whether to come back later.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You're through the door and someone reaches for your phone.

exchanges.notes: Standard in Berlin clubs. No photos inside, the tape stays until you leave, and people relax because of it.

situation.en: It's cold outside and you don't want to carry your coat all night.

answers.en: Cloakroom's on the right, three euros.

situation.en: You're stepping outside for air and they offer you a stamp.

likelyReply.en: See you in a bit, then.

situation.en: You're talking to people at the bar and want to keep it going.
This place is dying and you'd rather go on with the people you've met.
Someone at the bar notices you're standing by yourself.

question.en: Are you here on your own?

situation.en: The group you've joined is leaving and you want to tag along.

question.en: Where are you going after this?

answers.es: In den Club um die Ecke.
answers.en: To the club round the corner.

situation.en: You've been talking for ten minutes and lost their name immediately.
Someone you've been talking to offers to get the next round.
It's late and you want to leave without it being a whole thing.

likelyReply.en: It was good — see you soon!

situation.en: The bar you're in is dead and you want a local's recommendation.

question.es: Kennst du hier einen guten Laden?
question.en: Do you know anywhere good round here?

answers.es: Zwei Straßen weiter, der ist besser.
answers.en: Two streets over — that one's better.

phrases.en: To pre-drink — literally "to pre-glow".
Closing time — largely theoretical in Berlin.
The bouncer — the person who decides how your night goes.
To dance it properly out of your system.
To go big tonight.
To go straight through until morning.
In one — downing a drink in a single go.
The after-work beer — an institution rather than an event.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody invites you out and you want to know about the bit before.

question.es: Wir sind um eins im Club.
question.en: We'll be at the club at one.

scenes.notes: Literally to pre-glow. Berlin clubs fill after midnight, so the flat beforehand is most of the evening.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A track everybody knows comes on and your friend is still at the table.

answers.en: Come on — let's go and dance.

scenes.notes: Not just tanzen: abtanzen is dancing it out of your system, properly and for a while.

situation.en: It's somebody's last night in the city and nobody has plans.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's five in the morning and somebody asks whether you're going home.

scenes.notes: Durchmachen is going through without sleeping, and in Berlin it is often the actual plan rather than an accident.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A tray of shots arrives and somebody is waiting for everyone to be ready.

scenes.notes: Ex is from the Latin. Auf ex is in one go, and it is what people say instead of counting down.

categories.title: How drunk are you? (Germany)
categories.description: The whole ladder, and the moments where you have to pick a rung out loud.

note.en: German grades drunkenness finely and nobody is coy about it. Naming your rung honestly is normal, and it is how people decide whether to put you in a taxi.

phrases.en: Tipsy, in the nicest way — from schwippen, to sway.
Merry — the polite one, safe at a work party.
To have had a few — literally "to have one sitting".
To be drunk — literally "to be blue".
Drunk — the standard, neutral word.
Plastered — informal, a bit crude, very common.
Hammered — Berlin's own, and said with some pride.
Falling-down drunk.
Someone who has gone under — literally a "schnapps corpse".
Completely gone.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Two glasses of Sekt in, somebody checks how you're getting on.

likelyReply.en: That stuff is stronger than it looks.

scenes.notes: From schwippen, to sway. The bottom of the scale and the nicest word on it.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A colleague at the office Christmas party asks whether you've had too much.

scenes.notes: The polite one, and the one to use at a work party. It says merry without admitting to drunk.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody asks how the friend asleep in the armchair ended up there.

question.es: Was ist denn mit ihm los?

likelyReply.en: We'll wake him in a minute.

scenes.notes: Literally to be blue, and nobody agrees why. Everyday, and said about somebody more often than about yourself.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's two in the morning and somebody is already on their way to the bar for you.

scenes.notes: Informal and a bit crude, and extremely common. Betrunken is what you'd write; besoffen is what you'd say.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone asks how your night in Kreuzberg ended.

scenes.notes: Berlin's own, and said with a certain amount of pride. Hacke alone does the job too.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody in the group can no longer stand up without help.

scenes.notes: Sturz is a fall, and the compound says exactly what it looks like.

situation.en: You've hit the point where the room has stopped being interesting.

question.es: Wir ziehen noch weiter, kommst du mit?

situation.en: A few drinks in, a friend checks how you're doing.

answers.en: All good — only two beers in.

situation.en: Someone is working out whether to order you another round.
You stand up and realize the room is doing something it shouldn't.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone arrives at the table with a tray of shots for everyone.

answers.es: Nee, ich bin schon gut dabei.
answers.en: Nah, I'm well on my way already.

exchanges.notes: "Gut dabei sein" is the graceful refusal — it admits you're drunk without making it a problem.

situation.en: You've hit your limit and want to stop before it stops you.

answers.es: Dann hör auf, ist doch okay.

situation.en: A stranger has noticed the state your friend is in.

answers.es: Der ist ziemlich besoffen, ich bring ihn heim.
answers.en: He's pretty plastered — I'm taking him home.

likelyReply.en: Do you two need a taxi?

situation.en: It's the next day and you're owning up to how last night went.

question.en: I was completely gone last night.

situation.en: You're leaving and someone wants to know you'll make it home.

question.en: Can you manage on your own?

situation.en: The round is going in and you'd rather sit this one out.
It's your round and you want something soft without a discussion.

question.es: Nur ein Wasser für mich, bitte.
question.en: Just a water for me, please.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You drove here and want that understood before anyone offers.

exchanges.notes: Germany's limit is 0.5, and 0.0 for your first two years of license. "Ich fahre" ends the conversation — nobody pushes.

situation.en: Someone won't take your first no about one more drink.
You've drunk more than you've eaten and you can feel it.
You've decided the night is over for you.
A friend is pacing you and pushes a glass of water over.
You're outside the bar and in no state to work out a night bus.

question.es: Kannst du mir ein Taxi rufen?
question.en: Could you call me a taxi?

categories.title: The morning after & the pharmacy (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: Your head is splitting and you need something for it.

question.en: Do you have anything for a headache?

situation.en: The pharmacist looks at you and asks what's wrong.

question.en: What seems to be the matter?

situation.en: You feel wrecked and want to explain why.

question.es: Ich hab die ganze Nacht nicht geschlafen.

situation.en: You want to know whether you need to see a doctor first.

question.en: Do I need a prescription for that?

situation.en: You're dehydrated and want something better than tap water.
Before handing anything over, the pharmacist checks what else you take.

question.en: Are you on any other medication?

situation.en: You've got the box and don't want to overdo it.

question.es: Wie oft soll ich das nehmen?
question.en: How often should I take this?

answers.en: Three times a day at most.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: It's Sunday and every pharmacy you've passed is shut.

answers.en: At the station — that one's on emergency duty.

exchanges.notes: German pharmacies shut evenings and Sundays. One per area runs a Notdienst rota, and every closed door lists which.

phrases.en: The hangover — literally "the tomcat".
Hungover.
The hangover breakfast — salty, and a genuine institution.
Hair of the dog — literally the "counter-beer".
A blackout — literally the film tearing mid-reel.
What's still in you this morning — the word that stops you driving.
To be desperately thirsty the day after — literally to have a fire.
Never again. Said sincerely, roughly monthly.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You appear in the kitchen at one in the afternoon and say nothing.

scenes.notes: Der Kater is the tomcat, and the hangover both. Probably from Katarrh rather than the animal, though nobody lets that get in the way.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody opens a beer at eleven the next morning and offers you one.

answers.en: Hair of the dog — why not.

scenes.notes: Literally the counter-beer. The theory is disputed; the practice is widespread.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend asks what happened after midnight and you have nothing at all.

question.es: Weißt du noch, was danach war?
question.en: Do you remember what happened after that?

scenes.notes: Literally the film tearing mid-reel, from the days when that happened in cinemas. The most vivid word in this section.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've drunk three glasses of water and are pouring a fourth.

scenes.notes: Literally to have a fire. It is the thirst specifically, not the headache.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend catches you swearing off alcohol for what must be the hundredth time.

question.es: Wie oft hast du das jetzt gesagt?
question.en: How many times have you said that now?

scenes.notes: Said with total sincerity, roughly monthly.

categories.title: Robbed, lost & emergencies (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You reach for your wallet on the U-Bahn and it isn't there.
You need to report it and don't know where to go.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: Your insurer needs a crime number before they'll pay out.

question.en: I'd like to file a report.

answers.es: Kommen Sie mit, ich nehme das auf.
answers.en: Come with me, I'll take it down.

exchanges.notes: The Anzeige is what your travel insurance will ask for. Do it before you leave the city.

situation.en: The officer taking your report asks what you saw.

question.en: Did you see who did it?

likelyReply.es: Wir schauen uns die Kameras an.

situation.en: Your passport is gone and your flight is tomorrow.
You've come out of a club alone and your group is nowhere.

question.es: Können Sie mir helfen? Ich finde meine Freunde nicht.
question.en: Can you help me? I can't find my friends.

answers.es: Bleiben Sie hier, wir suchen sie.
answers.en: Stay here, we'll look for them.

situation.en: Someone in your group is hurt and needs seeing to.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: A stranger has stopped to help and is reaching for their phone.

exchanges.notes: 112 is the Europe-wide emergency number: free, works from any phone, and works without a SIM.

situation.en: Your phone died and you have no way to call anyone.
You're asking around the bar for a charger.
You need to reach someone and your phone is useless.

question.en: Could I make a quick call?

situation.en: You have no data and need to look up where you are.

answers.es: Ja, Passwort steht an der Wand.

situation.en: Roaming is costing you a fortune and you want a local SIM.

question.es: Kannst du mir eine SIM-Karte empfehlen?
question.en: Can you recommend a SIM card?

answers.en: At the phone shop in the station.

situation.en: You're standing on a corner looking visibly lost and someone stops.

likelyReply.en: Where are you trying to get to?

situation.en: The trains have stopped and you need any way home at all.

question.en: How do I get out of here?

answers.en: Night bus M10, just up there.

situation.en: The bar is cash-only and your pockets are empty.

answers.en: There's a cash machine in the Späti.

categories.title: For the girls (Germany)
categories.description: What it sounds like, and how to end it.

note.en: Every line here is meant to be said at normal volume or louder. Germans will not think you are overreacting — bar and club staff are trained for exactly this.

subsections.title: What it sounds like & shutting it down

situation.en: A man you don't know steps into your path outside a bar.

question.en: Hey gorgeous, all on your own?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone tells you to smile as you walk past.

question.en: Come on, give us a smile!

exchanges.notes: The comeback is the tell: a man who calls you a Zicke for declining was never being friendly.

situation.en: Someone has been talking at you for five minutes and won't take a hint.

question.en: I want to be left alone.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: A stranger puts a hand on your waist in a crowded bar.

exchanges.notes: Say it loudly. The volume is the point — it turns heads, and that is what makes it stop.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: A man insists on buying you a drink you didn't ask for.

answers.en: Thanks, I've already got a drink.

exchanges.notes: Never accept a drink you didn't watch being poured, however well it's meant.

situation.en: Polite has stopped working and you're done being polite.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You get the bartender's attention about the man who won't leave.

exchanges.notes: German bar staff will act on this. Say it to them rather than to your friends.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You want the fastest exit line, whether or not it's true.

question.es: Ich bin mit meinem Freund hier.

exchanges.notes: It shouldn't work better than no. It often does. Use whatever ends it fastest.

situation.en: You want someone with you between the door and the taxi.

question.es: Kannst du mich zum Taxi bringen?
question.en: Can you walk me to a taxi?

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: Nothing has happened yet but you want to leave anyway.

question.es: Ich fühl mich hier nicht wohl.

exchanges.notes: You never have to justify this one. "Nicht wohl" is reason enough for any German friend.

situation.en: You don't want to be on your own for the next few minutes.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: Two sips in, your drink has hit you far harder than it should have.

question.es: Ich glaube, mir wurde was ins Glas getan.
question.en: I think something was put in my drink.

exchanges.notes: Tell the bar staff, not only your friends. German clubs take this seriously and have a procedure for it.

situation.en: A bartender has clocked that something is wrong and offers to step in.
You're leaving alone and want someone to know you got back.

question.es: Ich schreib dir, wenn ich zu Hause bin.
question.en: I'll text you when I'm home.

situation.en: He's waiting outside and you'd rather not walk out yet.

question.es: Kann ich hier warten, bis er weg ist?
question.en: Can I wait here until he's gone?

answers.en: Of course — as long as you like.

situation.en: Your group is drifting toward the door and you don't want to be last.
